observation.short: An observation is what you can point to: color, shape, water, time. It is not yet a story about why.
observation.more: If you cannot show it on the ground or in a measurement you took, it is not an observation yet. A carrying story can wait until the notes hold it.

interpretation.short: Interpretation is the story you attach after the notes exist. It can be wrong even when the observation is real.
interpretation.more: Sorting seen vs guessed is the habit: keep the sentence you can still point to, and hold the cause loosely until more notes agree.

evidence.short: Evidence is a note you actually collected that can support or weaken a claim.
evidence.more: A real note can still be the wrong note for this claim. Wren is asking whether this evidence answers this question — not whether you visited a place.

variable.short: A variable is the one thing you change on purpose so you can see what it does.
variable.more: On the runoff table the tested variable is slope. Water amount is a different change. Change both at once and you cannot say which one mattered.

fair-test.short: A fair test changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, and repeats the run.
fair-test.more: One trial can be a fluke. Two or more on each slope, same cup of water, is a comparison you can defend.

runoff.short: Runoff is rainwater moving over the ground instead of soaking in right away.
runoff.more: Steeper, looser ground sheds water faster. Flatter, vegetated, or marshy ground holds it longer. That difference shows up as travel time and as a muddy pulse.

slope.short: Slope is how steep the ground is. Water on a steeper slope usually gets where it is going sooner.
slope.more: Gravity pulls downhill. Steepness changes the speed, not the direction. Direction still follows the fall of the land.

gravity.short: Gravity pulls water downhill. It does not pull water up Granite Knob.
gravity.more: Rills, outlets, and tributaries are the map of that pull. If a story needs water to climb, the land is disagreeing.

pattern.short: A pattern is what repeats in numbers or places you actually recorded — not a one-off.
pattern.more: On the runoff graph, look at whether steeper channels keep finishing sooner across trials. One fast run is not yet a pattern.

system.short: A system is parts that work together in one event: source, path, store, and what got hit.
system.more: Last night's rain, the Westface scar, Fox Run, the marsh, and the willows are not four separate stories. Change one part and the downstream response can change.

storage.short: Storage holds water for a while. It can change timing without starting the flood.
storage.more: The marsh stays wet most days. That is not the same as the brown pulse that rode Fox Run after the slope failed.

downstream.short: Downstream is the direction water already chose — toward lower ground.
downstream.more: A change on Westface shows up later at the join, then the pond, then further creek. The station reach can stay relatively clear if the pulse took a tributary instead.

timescale.short: A timescale is how long a process needs. Last night is one clock. The mismatched boulder needs a longer one.
timescale.more: A rain can move sand and mud. It does not park a boulder that does not match the hill. Those notes can both be true.

revision.short: Revision is dropping a cause that the land disagrees with — not adding every brown place to the story.
revision.more: A first story that never broke is not revision. When a crate note or a clear reach conflicts, the honest move is to narrow the case.

cause.short: A cause is what actually made the change. Being nearby is not enough.
cause.more: Willows took a hit. They did not call the storm. Rain fell widely. The pulse still needed a loose slope and a path.

correlation.short: Two things can happen together without one causing the other.
correlation.more: It rained and the willows look torn. The rain still does not make trees the engine of the pulse. Ask which part moved the water.
